idiom_name: Vapor middleware over the Cache protocol (app.caches / req.cache), with Leaf's production template cache
implementation_notes: Server-side Swift assembles the pattern from Vapor's parts: an AsyncMiddleware wrapping the responder derives a key from method, URI and the vary axes, asks the request- or application-scoped cache (req.cache / app.caches, filled by a store registered on the application) for the stored Response, returns it on a hit and stores the fresh response on a miss, letting the store own TTL and eviction; Leaf, Vapor's template engine, separately keeps its compiled/rendered templates in a cache that is enabled in production and disabled in development, which removes part of the rendering cost even for pages that are not themselves cached. Response is a value type in Vapor, so a cached entry is simply the response plus its expiry, and Swift's value semantics make accidental mutation of a shared cached body far harder than in reference-object languages - the remaining work is still the store's bounds, the key and the purge path.
pitfalls: Vapor's default in-memory store is per process and has no eviction policy of its own: unbounded keys (slugs, query strings) grow the process until a TTL- or size-limited store (or Redis) is configured.

Caching a Response that sets cookies or was produced from an Authorization header serves one user's session to the next request; check method/status and vary on the personalisation axes before storing.
Async middleware must not block the event loop - use the async/EventLoopFuture cache API and await the store instead of doing synchronous file or database work inside respond(to:chainingTo:).
